For adsorption on transition-metal surfaces modeled by periodic plane-wave density functional theory, where the exchange-correlation energy is approximated by the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof generalized-gradient functional and total energies E are computed with the Vienna ab initio Simulation Package using a plane-wave cutoff energy of 400 eV and a (4×4×1) Monkhorst–Pack k-point mesh for a surface supercell, the resulting adsorption-energy differences between metals are sufficiently accurate that trends in binding energies of CO2, CO, and atomic O can be treated as physically meaningful descriptors despite systematic functional errors.
      [47,48,49]

The Perdew–Wang generalized-gradient approximation (PW91), defined here as the semilocal generalized-gradient exchange-correlation functional of Perdew and Wang used within Kohn–Sham density-functional theory to evaluate the electronic total energy $E_{\text{tot}}[n(\mathbf{r})]$ for a given electronic density $n(\mathbf{r})$, is assumed to yield adsorption energies $E_{\text{ad}}$, alloy formation energies (total-energy differences between alloyed and separated-reference configurations), and transition-state barrier heights for palladium–vanadium (Pd–V) surface systems and for CO adsorption on Pd(111) that are accurate to within approximately $0.1$–$0.3\ \text{eV}$ of higher-level (for example, hybrid-functional or many-body) reference methods for similar metal-surface problems; this level of accuracy justifies interpreting the calculated energetic orderings reported here (hollow < bridge < top adsorption-site ranking, exothermic incorporation versus endothermic adsorption, and the relative formation-energy ranking of surface superstructures) without introducing additional empirical corrective schemes.

Kohn–Sham density functional theory calculations performed with commonly used generalized-gradient-approximation (GGA) exchange-correlation functionals on periodic metal-surface slab models produce adsorption energies and estimated activation energies for chemisorbed intermediates and transition states that are inherently approximate and can carry systematic errors on the order of a few tenths of an electronvolt (approximately 0.1–0.3 eV) depending on the adsorbate, surface, and reaction coordinate; therefore, computed energetic differences that are comparable in magnitude to these typical DFT error bars should be treated with caution. In this proposition, 'GGA exchange-correlation functional' denotes the family of approximate functionals in Kohn–Sham DFT that include gradient corrections to the local density approximation, 'adsorption energy' denotes the computed total-energy difference between the slab+adsorbate system and separated slab plus gas-phase species, and 'activation energy' denotes the DFT total-energy difference between a transition-state structure and the initial-state structure as optimized within the same DFT setup.

For the density functional calculations reported here the generalized-gradient-approximation Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof exchange–correlation functional (PBE; denoted $E_{xc}^{\mathrm{PBE}}[\rho]$) was used without any explicit dispersion correction (no DFT-D or van der Waals density functional), and this level of theory typically reproduces Born–Oppenheimer potential-energy differences (adsorption energies and activation barriers) for small organic adsorbates on late-transition-metal surfaces to within characteristic deviations on the order of $0.1$–$0.3\ \text{eV}$ for this class of systems.

The electronic structure calculations that yield the adsorption energies used the generalized‑gradient approximation Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (GGA‑PBE) exchange‑correlation functional within Kohn–Sham density functional theory and the projector‑augmented‑wave (PAW) method for electron–ion interactions; it is established for CO chemisorption on transition‑metal surfaces that semi‑local GGA‑PBE frequently produces systematic quantitative errors in adsorption energies (errors up to roughly 0.2–0.6 eV depending on the metal and adsorption site) and in some cases incorrect adsorption‑site energy ordering, so the absolute E_{\mathrm{ads}} values obtained with PBE are subject to known functional‑dependent systematic uncertainty.

The Perdew--Burke--Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized-gradient-approximation exchange-correlation functional, when used within Kohn--Sham density functional theory with projector-augmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotentials and a plane-wave basis, is assumed here to provide adsorption energies for molecular water adsorbed on late transition-metal close-packed surfaces (explicitly: Au(111), Ag(111), Pt(111), Pd/Au(111), Ru(0001)) that are accurate to within chemical accuracy (approximately $\pm 0.05\ \mathrm{eV}$) relative to the true ground-state adsorption energetics that would include all many-body correlation and dispersion effects not explicitly treated by PBE.

All reported adsorption-site energetics and series-wide binding-energy trends are obtained using the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof generalized-gradient-approximation exchange-correlation functional (PBE-GGA) within Kohn–Sham density-functional theory, and the computational conclusions assume that PBE-GGA provides sufficiently accurate total-energy differences (binding energies and site energy orderings) for 4d and 5d transition-metal adatoms on graphene such that systematic errors of PBE-GGA (including its approximate treatment of exchange, correlation, and self-interaction for localized d electrons) do not qualitatively change the reported adsorption-site preferences and series trends.

The Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized-gradient-approximation exchange-correlation functional used in the density-functional-theory calculations reproduces the electronic structure, equilibrium adsorption geometries, adsorption energies, transition-state energies, and qualitative charge-redistribution trends for molecular H2 interacting with both clean and transition-metal-doped Al(111) surface models to an accuracy on the order of chemical accuracy (approximately ±0.1 eV for energetics), so that PBE-level results reliably determine the direction and relative magnitudes of the catalytic barrier changes reported in this work.

The DFT reference adsorption formation energies used as ground truth were computed with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized-gradient-approximation exchange–correlation functional including Grimme D2 dispersion corrections (PBE-D2), and the cited benchmarking literature indicates that common GGA-level DFT functionals have typical adsorption-energy errors on the order of ~0.2 eV relative to higher-level benchmarks for transition-metal adsorption, which is comparable to the MAE scale reported for the machine-learning models.
      Wellendorff et al., Surf. Sci. benchmark (cited in main text and refs 79)

For adsorption-energy calculations of single neutral Pb, Ni, and Pt atoms on a periodic slab model of the $\gamma$-alumina (110) surface in vacuum, the Kohn-Sham density functional theory approximation in which the exchange-correlation energy is described by the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof generalized-gradient-approximation functional is treated as sufficiently accurate to support energetic rankings and mechanistic conclusions despite known systematic errors of the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional for transition-metal/oxide chemisorption.

All reported adsorption energies (for example, the $9.43\ \text{eV}$ D3 value for Ti on a boron-substituted $4\times2$ graphene supercell) were computed with Kohn–Sham density functional theory using the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized-gradient exchange-correlation functional and the projector-augmented-wave (PAW) method, with a plane-wave kinetic-energy cutoff of $400\ \text{eV}$ and Brillouin-zone k-point samplings of $14\times1\times1$ for the $2\times2$ cell and $7\times14\times1$ for the $4\times2$ cell; the quantitative conclusion that the Ti adsorption energy on boron-substituted graphene substantially exceeds the Ti bulk cohesive energy therefore rests on the numerical accuracy of the PBE/PAW Kohn–Sham DFT calculations for transition-metal–surface bonding and for metal bulk cohesive energies carried out in finite periodic supercells. Table I

For adsorption energies defined as $E_{ads}=E_{\text{surface/adsorbate}}-E_{\text{surface}}-E_{\text{adsorbate}}$, where the three total energies are obtained from the same Kohn–Sham density functional theory (KS-DFT) numerical setup, the proposition is that the exchange–correlation functional Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) within the generalized-gradient approximation combined with Grimme's semiempirical DFT-D dispersion correction, together with a plane-wave basis truncated at a kinetic-energy cutoff of $330\ \mathrm{eV}$ and a Monkhorst–Pack Brillouin-zone sampling grid of $6\times6\times1$ for the surface supercell, produces adsorption energies $E_{ads}$ whose systematic errors relative to better-converged numerical settings or higher-level electronic-structure treatments (for example, larger plane-wave cutoff, denser $k$-point sampling, hybrid exchange functionals, or many-body methods) are small enough that the qualitative ranking of adsorption sites and the large binding-energy differences reported in this work (differences of several tenths to roughly $1\ \mathrm{eV}$) are not altered by those higher-accuracy changes.

Periodic DFT calculations performed with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof generalized gradient approximation exchange–correlation functional (PBE-GGA), Troullier–Martins norm-conserving pseudopotentials, and a finite localized atomic orbital basis set consisting of double-zeta plus polarization (DZP) functions with basis localization radii chosen from an energy shift of $0.01\ \mathrm{eV}$ and a real-space mesh cutoff of $200\ \mathrm{Ry}$ produce adsorption energies for small adsorbates on close-packed transition-metal surfaces that typically carry an intrinsic methodological uncertainty on the order of $5\ \mathrm{kcal/mol}$ (≈0.2 eV) in absolute adsorption energies when compared to higher-level references or alternative DFT setups; here the symbol $Q$ denotes the adsorption energy defined as the total-energy difference $Q=E_{\text{adsorbate+slab}}-E_{\text{clean slab}}-E_{\text{gas-phase adsorbate}}$ computed with the stated pseudopotential, functional, and basis settings.
      Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof, Phys. Rev. Lett. 77, 3865 (1996); Troullier & Martins, Phys. Rev. B 43, 8861 (1991)

For periodic density functional theory calculations of adsorption and binding energetics for transition-metal dimers supported on oxide slabs, using the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof generalized-gradient-approximation exchange–correlation functional (PBE) together with projector augmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotentials yields relative total-energy differences between competing adsorbate geometries that are sufficiently reliable that the identity of the lowest-energy structure and the reported energy separations between low-energy structures are not qualitatively altered by typical exchange–correlation functional errors.

Let the benchmark reference adsorption energy for reaction i be E_i^{ref}, taken from the Wellendorff et al. compilation of experimental adsorption energies after conversion to vibrationless Born–Oppenheimer energies and assignment of adsorption site and coverage. The proposition is that these experimental E_i^{ref} values and the associated assignments of adsorption site and coverage are sufficiently accurate and precise to serve as reliable references for benchmarking density functionals on the 39 selected transition-metal surface systems, assuming that experimental uncertainties due to surface defects, site misassignments, coverage-dependent energetics, or conversion corrections are small compared to the functional errors used for comparative evaluation.
      Ref. 1

A density functional theory calculation using the B3LYP exchange–correlation functional (the hybrid generalized-gradient-approximation functional combining Becke three-parameter exchange and Lee–Yang–Parr correlation) applied to a finite metal cluster model Au_{5}Pd_{5} with one adsorbed propene molecule yields an electronic-structure adsorption energy that serves as a reference value for small Au–Pd cluster motifs; this B3LYP adsorption energy is expected to be a reliable approximation to the true electronic adsorption energy within typical "chemical accuracy" bounds of approximately 0.05–0.10 eV for physisorption energetics and therefore is an appropriate computational benchmark for parametrizing or validating the classical interatomic potentials used to model propene–metal physisorption in the MD work.

All DFT total energies used to build the PESs were computed with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized-gradient-approximation exchange-correlation functional, and it is assumed that the PBE functional yields adsorption energies and diffusion-barrier heights for atomic hydrogen on the studied transition-metal (100) and (111) surfaces with errors small enough (relative to the reported intermetal trends and numerical ranges of ≈0.01–1.7 eV) that the conclusions about motif identification and relative barrier magnitudes remain valid. J. P. Perdew, K. Burke, and M. Ernzerhof, Phys. Rev. Lett. 77, 3865 (1996).

Periodic plane-wave Kohn–Sham density functional theory calculations were performed using the PW91 generalized-gradient approximation (GGA) for the exchange–correlation functional, ultrasoft pseudopotentials to represent all ionic cores, Fermi smearing of the electronic occupations with k_{B}T = 0.1 eV (followed by extrapolation of total energies to k_{B}T = 0), and a plane-wave kinetic-energy cutoff of 25 Ry; these settings produce adsorption free energies G_{X^*} (Gibbs free energies of species X adsorbed on a specified close-packed metal slab surface) that, for the set of carbon- and oxygen-containing methanol-decomposition intermediates and the twelve transition-metal surfaces considered, are estimated to be accurate to within approximately ±0.10 eV (chemical accuracy) for relative adsorption energetics and trends.

For periodic-slab density-functional theory calculations performed with the generalized-gradient approximation variant GGA-RPBE for the exchange–correlation functional, ultrasoft pseudopotentials, and a plane-wave basis set with kinetic-energy cutoff $25\ \mathrm{Ry}$, the computed absolute adsorption energies $\Delta E$ (defined here as the dissociative chemisorption potential energy of the dissociation products measured relative to the free gas-phase molecule) and transition-state energies $E_a$ (defined here as the transition-state energy for dissociation measured relative to the free gas-phase molecule) are expected to be accurate to within approximately a few tenths of an electronvolt for representative transition-metal surfaces and diatomic adsorbates, with systematic errors from the choice of functional and incomplete basis/pseudopotential convergence typically at the $0.1$–$0.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ level and capable of shifting both $\Delta E$ and $E_a$ in a correlated or uncorrelated manner depending on the system; this methodological assessment is discussed in the cited methodological study.
      16

The Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized-gradient-approximation exchange-correlation functional, defined as the approximation $E_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{PBE}}[\rho]$ to the Kohn–Sham density-functional-theory exchange-correlation energy as a functional of the electron density $\rho(\mathbf{r})$, is assumed to yield cohesive energies, harmonic phonon frequencies, activation barriers for O$_2$ dissociation, magnetic exchange energetics, and electronic band classifications (metal versus semiconductor versus half-metal) with sufficient quantitative accuracy for one-dimensional phosphorus nanowires and transition-metal-decorated phosphorus sandwich chains to support the stated stability and electronic/magnetic assignments obtained at the PBE level.
